title: How Does it All Fit Together?
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart reflects on how various Buddhist teachings and practices from different cultures and traditions don't necessarily fit together seamlessly, but instead form a rich tapestry shaped by cultural exchange and adaptation over time. They explore how Buddhism has evolved in new contexts, incorporating local customs and influences, and how the six perfections (generosity, discipline, patience, energy, meditation, and wisdom) relate to the Noble Eightfold Path, highlighting the importance of wisdom as a foundation for spiritual practice.

sentences.text: Dear Dharma friends, I think this is the last installment of our Dharma conversation series that is taking place around the practice period.
It was really wonderful to practice with people in person after such a long time of solo practice in front of the screen.
I also confess it kind of messed me up a bit, because I was used to one person doing everything and I couldn't quite remember who was doing what.
This was great humility practice.
I want to really thank Hannah for having been Shusou, and Karen for being Benji, and Talis for being Kokyo, and Bob Tenkin and Raizelah Doan and Tim Doshi and everybody who was showing up.
It felt really great.
So thank you very much.
What I wanted to talk about today actually came from a Doku-san I had a while ago.
Someone said to me, "I really don't get how all our practices and teachings fit together.
We have the precepts, we have the Four Noble Truth, we have the emptiness teachings, we have the koans, we study Dogen, we study the Brahma Viharas and so on.
How does it all fit together?"
I tried to answer and realized it's actually pretty complicated, the way what we do and what we study, what we work with.
Oh, and another thing came up, which is our robes.
Where do they come from?
Why do we dress so funny and awkward?
I'll start with that, because the theme of cultural appropriation also came up around it.
Yes, it is cultural appropriation.
The koromo with the big huge sleeves is actually a Confucian scholar robe from China.
The kimono that's in juban worn underneath, they're from Japan.
Our okesa comes from India, the [unclear: "I'm having on right now from Costco"].
So it's really a cultural mix.
The person who was talking about cultural appropriation said, well, here in the West it's cultural appropriation to wear this.
But then we should go back further.
It was cultural appropriation that people in China wore okesas and that people in Japan were wearing Confucian scholar clothing.
It is our tradition, and I don't argue with it a whole lot.
I don't see how I'm doing injury to someone by wearing it.
So that's the clothing part.
And then what we study.
I try to get an assembly together of things we read.
So this is a copy of the [unclear: "Middle East discourses"] from the Pali Canon, and those are the closest we have to the words of the Buddha.
This is the original.
Then we have scriptures like the Diamond Sutra, which we just studied, the Avatamsaka Sutra, the Lotus Sutra, which are Mahayana Sutras.
They were probably written a bit later; there seems to be consensus around that.
Then we have Koan literature.
This is the Book of Serenity, which is more or less 100 Zen dialogues, a little bit more Soto Zen oriented.
We have the Blue Cliff Record and the Mumonkan, which come more from the Rinzai tradition.
We have things like Shantideva's Way of the Bodhisattva.
We have Tibetan teachings like the [unclear: "Lo Chung"] slogans that we've studied.
Then there's always Dogen.
And then we have hundreds and hundreds of books that are commentaries on all the things that I mentioned before.
Western psychology and neurology is entering the field too.
Mindfulness teachings are actually from one of the Sutras, the Satipatthana Sutra, the Mindfulness Sutra, expanded into Western thinking and understanding of behavioral science and brain science.
And then, like I said before, tons of commentaries on all of the above.
And then we look at all these teachings, and we find that they really don't mesh that seamlessly.
If you Google it, and I can probably find this again, I printed this out a while ago: this is the Five Minute Buddhist.
These are cliff notes.
There are the five skandhas, the five aggregates, matter, sensation, perception, formation, consciousness, that we just chanted in the Heart Sutra.
Then we have the Four Noble Truths, which we also referenced in the Heart Sutra.
Then we have the Eightfold Path.
We often talk about the Brahma Viharas, the Four Sublime States.
We talk about our precepts.
We talk about the Paramita Perfections.
And [unclear: "how does it end the Eightfold Path"]?
None of it really seamlessly meshes from one into the other.
We can thank the long journey throughout space and time that Buddhism has undertaken in the last 2,500 years.
It's covered a lot of ground.
The interesting thing, I thought, was that Buddhism has always changed significantly when it has entered a new culture.
I think culture is a better word than country.
If you read the Buddha's Pali Canon, it is very flowery.
It is very much the jungle climate, the plains of the Ganges.
That created scriptures like the Flower Ornament Sutra; it stems from that feeling of that culture.
In China, our lineages were created, or I should say maybe emphasized.
All of a sudden, it became very important how the teachings were transmitted and who the spiritual father of the teacher was.
I don't think it was that emphasized in India, but the result is that we received these beautiful lineage papers when we do the Chukai.

And then Japan: the culture of Japan definitely influences very much our Soto Zen tradition, our forms and our formality, that we appreciate a certain exactness and precision and totally appreciate every mistake that's being made.
Because only in those mistakes can we have a feeling for our forms.
It would really scare me if something went 100% perfect throughout everything.
One thing I really wanted to talk about was the six perfections, which are fundamental in our teaching: generosity, discipline, patience, energy, meditation, and wisdom.
It really interested me how they relate to the Noble Eightfold Path, which is part of the Four Noble Truth.
The Eightfold Path is right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
And what I found very interesting is this.
A lot of people try to gain an understanding of both the paramitas, the perfections, and the Noble Eightfold Path as a step-by-step program.
So first work on generosity, and then go to discipline, and so on, and so on.
The Eightfold Path is the same: first, get a right view, and then right intention, right speech.
And then there are some other people who look at both more like an octopus, so that each one is equally important, and there is no "this first and that," no series, but you take it on as a whole.
What really interested me, and what I would like to talk about in our Dharma conversation, is that in the six perfections, the last one is wisdom.
And in the Eightfold Path, right view, which is like the wisdom equivalent, is the first.

I find that very interesting, because when I read commentaries on the paramitas, it says, "Oh, it's really important that you get everything in place before you even attempt to practice the wisdom teachings."
And when I read commentaries on the Eightfold Path, they say, "Right view, wisdom: it's really important that you get that first, because if you don't have that, how can you practice anything else?
Everything is based on your understanding, on the wisdom aspect of the Eightfold Path.
If you don't have that right, everything else is going to be off."
So I find this almost endearing, how people really invest themselves in it being first and last.
And I'm not even going into the [unclear: "presets"] because we've all studied those.
So that is the jumping off point for our Dharma conversation.
And if this doesn't speak to you, if you'd rather talk about the journey of Buddhism, feel free, whatever inspires you.
Thank you very much.
And tell us, if you could stop the recording, that would be great.
